newsitem.title: CHINA: CHINA RULER MUST BE TIGER TO SUCCEED DRAGON DENG.
newsitem.headline: CHINA RULER MUST BE TIGER TO SUCCEED DRAGON DENG.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin grabbed centre stage on Tuesday to face the 1.2 billion people he now rules and the inscrutable opponents he now confronts without his patron Deng Xiaoping. Can he hold the spotlight?

With farewell rites completed for the communist strongman, Jiang stands unprotected in the cut-throat world of Chinese politics to prove whether he is a dragon like his late protector or merely a paper tiger, diplomats said.
"We will have to see if the tiger is one of paper -- or not," said one Western diplomat.

Jiang, 70 and born in the Chinese year of the tiger, emerged last week with the death of Deng from under the vast shadow cast by the diminutive revolutionary who was born in the most auspicious of China's lunar calendar years -- the dragon.
"He's got a way to go before he puts his position beyond challenge," said a second diplomat.

The Soviet-trained technocrat who holds China's top three posts -- Communist Party chief, state president and commander-in-chief of the armed forces -- appears to have negotiated a seamless succession to Deng, who died last Wednesday at 92 after ruling China for 18 years.
His face was the first that China saw on state television when the nation paused for three minutes on Tuesday to pay its respects to Deng in a ceremony in the Great Hall of the People.

His destiny as Deng's heir was the theme of a collage of some of Deng's last public television appearances in the early 1990s that state television chose to broadcast in the minutes before the start of Tuesday's memorial rites.

"It's like after Mao Zedong died, when all the publicity was focused on his successor Hua Guofeng," said one Chinese analyst. "But look what happened to him (Hua), he was thrown out within two years by Deng."

Most diplomats and analysts say Jiang appears to have got off to a firm start -- he has had seven years under Deng's wing to build up his power base in a system where the transfer of power depends more on who you know than what job you have.

Delivering the eulogy, Jiang stood in the Great Hall of the People on Tuesday, Deng's ashes in a casket behind him draped with the hammer-and-sickle communist flag and facing 10,000 people -- among them ambitious pretenders to the power he now holds and presumably the ill-fated Hua Guofeng.
Waiting in the wings are head of parliament Qiao Shi, 72, Premier Li Peng, 68, high-spirited Politburo member Li Ruihuan, 62, and ex-military former state president Yang Shangkun, still spry at 89.

Jiang was careful to avoid using the eulogy to promote his own position, but on a balcony above him hung a banner reading: "Under the party's leadership with Jiang Zemin as its core, carry out the unfulfilled wishes of Deng Xiaoping."
Diplomats and analysts said Jiang may, even in the six days of mourning following Deng's death, have already committed errors by trying to step into his mentor's shoes too quickly.
Jiang has disobeyed Deng by placing his pale, puffy corpse on televised display in a carefully choreographed and emotion-packed final farewell with wailing relatives and weeping soldiers.
"He may be playing a game to bring on an internal shake-up himself, or he could be in trouble," said Sinologist Geremie Barme. "Something's brewing."
"Deng's death has once again given China the opportunity for political intrigues," said one Western diplomat.
"Nineteen ninety-seven is going to be a fascinating year," he said, adding that Jiang faces a party congress later this year when the party leader must be elected -- or re-elected if Jiang wins.
"Jiang Zemin, who while Deng Xiaoping was alive was the young successor, has become at the moment of Deng's death the incumbent leader who is immediately faced with a succession crisis," said Barme.
